'''''Parsonsia heterophylla''''', commonly called '''New Zealand jasmine''' or '''kaihua''', is a climbing plant [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[New Zealand]].<ref name=":4" /> It was first described by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Alan Cunningham]] in 1839.<ref name="powo">{{Cite web |title=''Parsonsia heterophylla'' A.Cunn. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:80926-1 |access-date=2024-02-17 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref name="cunn">{{cite journal |last=Cunningham |first=A. |date=1839 |title=Specimen of the Botany of New Zealand:Apocynaceae |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2278111 |journal=Annals of Natural History |volume=2 |pages=46}}</ref>

The name ''heterophylla'' comes from the differing leaf shapes that can be seen in seedlings and juvenile plants of the species.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Moore |first=Lucy B.|title=The Oxford book of New Zealand plants|date=1978|publisher=Oxford University Press|others=J. B. Irwin|isbn=0-19-558035-4|location=Wellington [N.Z.]|oclc=3844208}}</ref> ''Heterophylla'' means varied leaves, from the Greek words ''heteros'' and ''phullon''.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=''Parsonsia heterophylla'' |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/parsonsia-heterophylla/ |access-date=2021-04-05 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |language=en}}</ref> Synonyms for this species include ''Parsonsia albiflora'' [[Etienne Raoul|Raoul]]<ref name="powo" /><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/56050392|journal=Annales des Sciences Naturelles, Botanique |series=Série 3 |volume=2|pages= 118 |date=1844|author=Raoul, E.F.L. |title=Plantes de la Nouvelle-Zelande}}</ref> ''and Parsonsia macrocarpa'' [[William Colenso|Colenso]].<ref name="powo" /><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute|volume= 14|pages= 320–339 [331] |date=1882|author=Colenso, W|title=Description of a few new Indigenous Plants |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/33980750}}</ref> It can also be described as "the varied-leaved ''Parsonsia''".<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last1=Laing|first1=Robert Malcolm|title=Plants of New Zealand|last2=Blackwell|first2=Ellen W.|publisher=Whitcombe and Tombs|year=1949|location=Christchurch New Zealand |pages=360}}</ref> There are 40 species of ''[[Parsonsia]]'' found in [[Asia]], [[Australasia]] and the Pacific. ''P. heterophylla'' is one of two endemic ''Parsonsia'' species found in New Zealand.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Smith-Dodsworth|first=John C.|title=New Zealand native shrubs and climbers|date=1991|publisher=David Bateman|isbn=1-86953-069-1|location=Auckland, N.Z.|oclc=27264960}}</ref> It is more robust and has bigger flowers than its close relative, ''[[Parsonsia capsularis]],'' which is also known as akakiore or small Māori jasmine.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|last=Salmon|first=John T. |title=New Zealand flowers and plants in colour|date=1986|publisher=Mural Books|isbn=0-9597795-0-7|oclc=33217447}}</ref>

''Parsonsia variabilis'' [[John Lindley|Lindl''.'']] is listed as a synonym by the [[New Zealand Plant Conservation Network]].<ref name=":3" /> However, [[International Plant Names Index|IPNI]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Parsonsia variabilis'' {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/81016-1 |access-date=2024-02-17 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref> and [[Plants of the World Online|Plants of the World online]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Parsonsia capsularis'' (G.Forst.) R.Br. ex Endl. (synonyms){{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:80887-1#synonyms |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> list ''Parsonsia variabilis'' as a synonym of  ''Parsonsia capsularis.''

==Description==
[[File:Parsonsia heterophylla kz11.jpg|left|thumb|267x267px|Flowers of ''Parsonsia heterophylla'']]
The flowers of ''P. heterophylla'' are "white, scented, and tubular with anthers hidden within the tube."<ref name=":0" /> This species has also been observed rarely to have yellow flowers.<ref name=":2" /> They appear in many-flowered, fairly compact clusters on the plant.<ref name=":2" /> The flowers are small, each usually up to 8mm in size.<ref name=":6" /> The flowers are often described for their peculiar scent.<ref name=":4" /> Often seen draped over the tops of tall trees, the flowers are more recognisable by their scent than their appearance.<ref name=":0" />

The fruit of ''P. heterophylla'' is a long, narrow pod that opens to release tufted seeds.<ref name=":0" /> These seeds pods are around 15 cm long.<ref name=":6" /> Each pod holds numerous seeds, and each one is tipped with a tuft of silky hairs.<ref name=":5" /> The two-valved pod opens from the tip downwards, bending outwards and raising seeds up so that their tufts can be caught by the wind.<ref name=":8" /> The fruit pods start green, turning to brown and then after the seeds have been dispersed, the dry, empty pods hang a long time on the plant.<ref name=":5" />
[[File:Parsonsia heterophylla kz8.jpg|left|thumb|260x260px|Long narrow leaf type]]

The leaves of ''P. heterophylla'' are variable in size and shape, both in all stages of its life.<ref name=":1" /> The leaves of seedlings and juvenile plants are largely diverse, and a range of small and round, long and narrow and irregularly shaped leaves can all be found mixed on the same plant.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Wilson|first=Hugh D.|title=Plant life on Banks Peninsula|date=2013|isbn=978-0-9583299-6-5|location=Cromwell, New Zealand|oclc=861302803}}</ref> In adults, the leaves are described as "opposite, rather shiny and rather dark green from above, much paler underneath, more or less smooth-edge but often somewhat wavy edged, more than 1 cm wide, often 2, 3, or 4 cm wide and up to 10cm long".<ref name=":2" /> While the leaves of adult plants are usually shorter and broader than in juveniles, they are still variable in shape.<ref name=":1" /> The leaf types can narrowly be defined as small round, long narrow and moderately broad and oblong.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Cockayne|first=Leonard|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.12016|title=New Zealand plants and their story. By L. Cockayne ...|date=1919|publisher=M.F. Marks, Govt. Printer|location=Wellington, N.Z.|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.12016}}</ref>
[[File:Parsonsia heterophylla in Auckland Botanic Gardens.jpg|left|thumb|257x257px|Small round leaf type]]

The twining stems of ''P. heterophylla'' are often tightly wrapped around host stems and are described as softly woody and flexible.<ref name=":2" /> In older plants, the stem is woody towards the base.<ref name=":1" /> Each stem is as thick as a quill and shining.<ref name=":7" /> This branching climber can reach up to 10 metres tall by climbing up any plant within reach.<ref name=":1" />

==Distribution==

''P. heterophylla'' is an [[Indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] or endemic species of New Zealand, meaning that it is not found anywhere else in the world.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Flora of New Zealand {{!}} Taxon Profile {{!}} Parsonsia heterophylla|url=http://nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Parsonsia-heterophylla.html|access-date=2021-04-05|website=nzflora.info}}</ref>

Its presence has been recorded in the North Island, South Island, [[Manawatāwhi / Three Kings Islands|Three Kings Islands]] and [[Stewart Island / Rakiura|Stewart Island]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Eagle|first=Audrey Lily|title=Eagle's 100 shrubs & climbers of New Zealand : companion volume to Eagle's 100 trees of New Zealand : botanical paintings & notes|date=1978|publisher=Collins|others=Audrey Lily Eagle|isbn=0-00-216932-0|location=Auckland|oclc=5727559}}</ref> It is commonly found across the country in lowland or low [[Montane ecosystems|montane]] forest.<ref name=":0" />  Its preferred habitat is forest margins and clearings in coastal scrub patches.<ref name=":6" /> It has been observed to grow side by side with its close relative ''[[Parsonsia capsularis]]'' in the [[Banks Peninsula]], where hybrids are sometimes encountered.<ref name=":2" />

==Life cycle==

There is little information available on the timeline and life cycle of this species. This plant flowers from September to March, followed by seed pods from February.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Salmon|first=John T.|title=Native New Zealand flowering plants|date=1991|publisher=Reed|isbn=0-7900-0684-7|location=Auckland [N.Z.]|oclc=26036266}}</ref> Seeds are dispersed then by the wind.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|author=Martin, William|title=The flora of New Zealand|date=1961|publisher=Whitcombe and Tombs|oclc=1191018}}</ref>

For planting ''P. heterophylla'' in gardens, the optimal time to collect seeds is between February and April.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Calendar for seed collecting - grasses, sedges, lilies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers|url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/get-involved/run-a-project/restoration-advice/native-plant-restoration/ecosource-seeds/collection-and-propagation-guide-grasses/calendar-for-seed-collecting-grasses/|access-date=2021-04-09|website=www.doc.govt.nz|language=en-nz}}</ref>

==Interactions==

''P. heterophylla'' twine their young stems around other plants in order and grow and climb towards the sunlight.<ref name=":6" />

''P. heterophylla'' is a host plant to a number of invertebrate species, including beetles, wasps, moths, butterflies, grasshoppers and sucking bugs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment tool: Database|url=https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/ReportForm.aspx?RecordId=126&Type=P&SortBy=Alpha&Biostatus=a,c,e,n|access-date=2021-04-05|website=plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz}}</ref>  The larvae of the moth ''[[Stigmella kaimanua]]'' feed on the leaves of ''P. heterophylla''.<ref name="Nepticuloidea">{{cite web|title=Stigmella kaimanua Donner & Wilkinson, 1989|url=http://nepticuloidea.info/category/nepticuloidea/stigmella/stigmella-new-zealand-species/stigmella-kaimanua|access-date=26 June 2016|website=Nepticulidae and Opostegidae of the world|publisher=Naturalis Biodiversity Center|archive-date=11 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811161719/http://nepticuloidea.info/category/nepticuloidea/stigmella/stigmella-new-zealand-species/stigmella-kaimanua|url-status=dead}}</ref> It also attracts the rare New Zealand ribbonwood aphid or ''[[Paradoxaphis plagianthi]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kean|first1=John|last2=Stufkens|first2=Marlon|date=January 2005|title=Phenology, population ecology, and rarity of the New Zealand ribbonwood aphid,Paradoxaphis plagianthi|journal=New Zealand Journal of Zoology|volume=32|issue=3|pages=143–153|doi=10.1080/03014223.2005.9518407|s2cid=83762940|issn=0301-4223|doi-access=free}}</ref> The sweet-scented flowers of ''P. heterophylla'' are attractive to night-flying moths.<ref name=":1" />

The nectar of ''P. heterophylla'' is eaten by the [[New Zealand bellbird]] or korimako.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Food preferences of the bellbird (Anthornis melanura) in native forest remnants on the Port Hills, Banks Peninsula, New Zealand|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281628513|access-date=2021-04-08 |website=ResearchGate|language=en}}</ref>

==Further information==

''P. heterophylla's'' current [[conservation status]] is not threatened, according to the [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]].<ref name=":3" />

The flowers of ''P. heterophylla'' were historically often bound by [[Māori people|Māori]] to the perches of bird-traps as a lure.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Māori Plant Use Database Plant Use Details of Parsonsia heterophylla|url=https://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?firstcome=firstcome&PKey=FA81C29F-243A-4921-8F30-8EA34BC15FD9|access-date=2021-04-08|website=maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz}}</ref>
